To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Maternal depression is associated with insecure/disorganised child–mother attachment, and this is associated with child internalising problems.

maternal depression and psychotic disorder have been found to have a negative impact on infant attachment, and that this may be mediated by a number of factors, including parenting behaviour, maternal attachment, and the presence of comorbidity.

maternal psychopathology has an impact on child–mother attachments and the role of these attachments in mediating the transmission of developmental and psychopathological risk to the child is unclear.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of maternal depression and psychosis on the mother–child relationship and child development.
the impact of maternal depression on the mother–child relationship and the child’s attachment security.
understanding how the mother–child relationship influences the development of children’s mental health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive evidence of the impact of maternal mental disorder on the attachment between mother and child.
maternal depression and psychotic disorder are associated with attachment insecurity in infants and young children and that this may be mediated by maternal parenting sensitivity and state of mind.
the evidence is not yet strong enough to support the idea that maternal psychopathology per se causes disorganised or disorientated infant attachment behaviour.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

maternal psychopathology has a negative impact on the mother–child attachment relationship, and this may have an impact on the child’s developmental outcomes, although the mechanisms by which this occurs are not yet fully understood.
attachment theory is a useful framework for understanding the impact of psychopathology on parenting, and for identifying the children who are most at risk of poor developmental outcomes.
the attachment relationship is a powerful determinant of children’s development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the attachment system can serve as a protective factor for infants and toddlers in families affected by maternal depression and psychosis.
maternal mental health problems are not only a cause of insecure attachment but also a consequence.

attachment is a key factor in mediating the transmission of risk to children of mothers with severe psychopathology, but that the role of attachment is likely to be mediated by the presence of comorbidity and contextual factors.
